market_context: United States; flavor-label definitions under FDA regulations
title: Natural vs Artificial Flavors: What Each Term Actually Means

seo.title: Natural vs Artificial Flavors: Meaning
seo.meta_description: Under U.S. rules, natural flavor describes flavoring whose significant function comes from specified natural-source materials; artificial flavor covers flavoring not derived from those sources. The terms do not rank healthfulness.
seo.search_intent: Explain the FDA definitions of natural and artificial flavor and what the labels do not imply about nutrition or safety.

excerpt: Natural and artificial flavor are regulatory origin categories, not health grades. A natural flavor must derive its flavoring function from source materials listed in FDA rules; an artificial flavor is one whose flavor comes from other sources.
content_html:
“Natural flavor” sounds wholesome and “artificial flavor” sounds synthetic, but the U.S. label is not a nutrition score. FDA defines the categories mainly by where the flavoring substance comes from, not by whether the finished food is healthy or minimally processed.

Natural flavor starts with a defined source

Federal rules describe natural flavor as essential oils, extracts, distillates, protein hydrolysates, and related flavoring preparations derived from sources such as spices, fruits, vegetables, edible yeast, herbs, meat, seafood, poultry, eggs, dairy, and fermentation products, when their significant function is flavor rather than nutrition.

Artificial flavor is the remainder of the definition

If a flavoring substance is not derived from the natural-source categories in the regulation, it falls under artificial flavor. That classification says where the flavor came from; it does not automatically tell you whether the molecule is more toxic, stronger, or nutritionally important.

The same aroma molecule can exist in both contexts

Vanillin illustrates the point. Vanilla beans contain vanillin naturally, but the same chemical structure can be produced from other raw materials. The source and manufacturing route affect how the flavor is labeled even when a key aroma molecule is chemically identical.

Neither term describes the whole food

A soda made with natural flavor can still be high in added sugar. A low-sodium food containing artificial flavor can still have a strong overall nutrition profile. Ingredients, serving size, and the Nutrition Facts panel answer questions that the flavor label cannot.

Read “natural” and “artificial” as source descriptions for flavoring—not as shortcuts for healthy versus unhealthy.

faq.question: Are natural flavors healthier than artificial flavors?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. The terms describe regulatory source categories rather than the nutritional quality of the finished food.

faq.question: Can the same flavor molecule be natural or artificial?
faq.answer: A chemically identical aroma compound can come from different sources, and the source and manufacturing route can affect how it is categorized on a label.

faq.question: Do natural flavors add nutrients?
faq.answer: Their significant function is flavor, not nutrition, so the term does not imply a meaningful nutrient contribution.
